source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory
finding: Generative and evaluative creative modes do not map cleanly onto Type 1 and Type 2. Generation uses both types. Exploration/evaluation looks mainly Type 2. A simple divergent=Type 1, convergent=Type 2 mapping is rejected.
numbers: No new data. Reviews Genoplore, BVSR, Gabora's theory, Nijstad's dual pathway.
quote: analytic processes may give rise to new ideas and insights
limits: Narrative review. Authors state there is little empirical work on shifting in humans.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code 'generate=fast, evaluate=slow'. Code the mode switch, but let each mode use both cheap and deliberate calls.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory (Nijstad et al. 2010 meta-analysis as reported)
finding: Dual-pathway model: flexibility (many categories, shifting) predicts originality more than persistence (depth within a category).
numbers: r=0.36 flexibility-originality vs r=0.12 within-category fluency-originality (Nijstad et al. meta-analysis, reported second-hand in the review).
limits: Second-hand figures; the original Nijstad paper was not opened. Persistence effect rises when originality is scored within a category.
agent_relevance: Favors an explorer operator that forces category switches (breadth) before depth. Persistence still helps within a chosen category.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory (Nijstad unpublished)
finding: Correlation between a person's flexibility measure and persistence measure falls over time on a task, hinting people entrench in one pathway instead of shifting.
numbers: Direction only (correlation decreases over time); no values given. Personal communication.
limits: Unpublished personal communication; weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Agent drift into one mode over a long run is plausible. A code-level switch with a forced counter guards against entrenchment.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory (dual-process caveats)
finding: Dual-process theory itself is contested: System 1 is not unitary, default-interventionist and parallel-competitive variants differ, and a third process may control the switch.
numbers: Cites Evans 2008, Stanovich 2009, Sloman 1996.
limits: Theoretical; no creativity-specific numbers.
agent_relevance: The switch controller (Stanovich's 'third process') is what our code plays. Supports doing it outside the model.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin 135(1)
finding: Delayed incubation gives a small positive gain on problem solving. No funnel-plot sign of publication bias.
numbers: 117 effect sizes, 3,606 participants, median n=25 per study, 85 of 117 positive. Weighted mean 0.29 (95% CI 0.21-0.39); unweighted adjusted mean 0.36 (CI 0.26-0.45). Cochran Q=173.99, df=113, p<.001.
limits: Small samples. Effect sizes heterogeneous. Pools insight, visual and 'creative' (divergent) problems.
agent_relevance: Incubation analogue (a pause or unrelated step between attempts) has a small but real expected benefit; do not expect big gains.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) moderators
finding: Problem type matters. Creative (multi-solution, divergent) problems gain most from incubation, more than linguistic or visual insight problems. Longer preparation before the break gives larger effects.
numbers: Regression across 117 studies; for creative problems a high-load interlude gave smaller effects than low-load or rest (coefficient differences about 0.91, p<.05, and 0.79, p=.08).
limits: Few creative-problem studies used rest; unbalanced design. Authors re-ran without them.
agent_relevance: Switch to the generative/wide-search mode after enough preparation (problem loaded), not before. Open-ended tasks benefit most.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) cognitive-demand finding
finding: For linguistic insight problems, a low-demand filler task beat rest. This argues against the 'conscious work/fatigue recovery' account and for diffuse associative access.
numbers: Low-load interlude gave the strongest incubation effect for linguistic problems; high-load interlude gave smaller effects.
quote: low demand tasks yielded a stronger incubation effect than did resting
limits: Interpretation is the authors' proposal (competition between controlled and automatic processes). Not directly tested.
agent_relevance: A light, diffuse side-task between solver passes (random association prompts) may beat idle waiting. Untested for LLMs.

source: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) On making the right choice: meta-analysis and large-scale replication of the unconscious thought advantage. Judgment and Decision Making 10(1)
finding: Large replication found no unconscious thought advantage over deliberation in multi-attribute choice.
numbers: N=399 (196 deliberation, 203 distraction as first condition); accuracy 55.61% vs 55.17%. Bayes factor about 7.83 in favor of the null. No gender effect.
limits: Choice tasks, not creativity tasks. The original claim is about decisions.
agent_relevance: The 'let unconscious processing do the work' half of dual-process creativity is weakly supported. Do not rely on a distraction step to improve choices.

source: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) On making the right choice: meta-analysis and large-scale replication of the unconscious thought advantage. Judgment and Decision Making 10(1) (meta-analysis part)
finding: Published UTA effects are mostly small-sample. High-precision studies show nil or a deliberation advantage.
numbers: 61 studies, n from 40 to 399, g from -0.74 to 1.48. Only 16 significant of 61 (12 pro-UTA, 4 pro-deliberation); 45 non-significant. Random-effects pooled g=0.15 (CI 0.03-0.26, p=.01) before correction for publication bias.
limits: Pooled estimate is before trim-and-fill correction.
agent_relevance: Treat Dijksterhuis-style unconscious-thought benefit as unproven; the safer design is explicit deliberation.

source: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) On making the right choice: meta-analysis and large-scale replication of the unconscious thought advantage. Judgment and Decision Making 10(1) (moderator account tested)
finding: The 'moderator account' (UTA appears only under special conditions such as word-search distraction) was tested by building the replication under conditions judged optimal. It still found no effect.
numbers: Fixed vs self-paced deliberation: 59.4% vs 56.9% correct in one order, 58.2% vs 61.9% in the other; no reliable mode difference. Decision time 37.7 vs 37.1 s, d=0.02.
limits: Proponents might still argue about conditions not covered.
agent_relevance: Do not tune the scaffold around a fragile 'incubation under distraction' moderator.

source: Benedek, Jauk, Sommer, Arendasy & Neubauer (2014) Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: common and differential involvement of executive functions. Intelligence 46
finding: Latent-variable test: divergent thinking depends on updating and inhibition but not on shifting.
numbers: Standardised paths to creativity: updating b=.29 (p<.001), inhibition b=.20 (p=.04), shifting about 0 (ns). To fluid intelligence: updating b=.53, inhibition .12 ns, shifting ns. Gf-creativity latent r=.45.
limits: Lab sample (German speakers, about 230 after exclusions); task-impurity of EF measures; EFs came out uncorrelated, unlike other studies.
agent_relevance: Controlled generation needs working-memory updating and suppression of obvious ideas, not switching speed. An agent needs an explicit 'ban the obvious answers' step plus memory of ideas already given.

source: Benedek, Jauk, Sommer, Arendasy & Neubauer (2014) Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: common and differential involvement of executive functions. Intelligence 46 (shared variance)
finding: Executive functions explain part, not all, of why intelligence and divergent thinking correlate. Openness adds more.
numbers: Adding EFs lowered Gf-creativity residual r from .45 to .34 (43% of shared variance). Adding openness: residual r=.29, p=.06. Openness predicts creativity b=.36 but not Gf.
limits: Residual correlation partly depends on measurement error and task choice.
agent_relevance: Raw reasoning power is not enough; a disposition for wide exploration (openness analogue, e.g. high-entropy sampling in the explorer) adds independent value.

source: Lee & Therriault (2013) The cognitive underpinnings of creative thought: latent variable analysis. Intelligence 41
finding: Associative fluency is the shared base of both divergent and convergent thinking. Divergent and convergent latent factors were unrelated.
numbers: N=265. Associative fluency predicts divergent b=.56 and convergent b=.82 (p<.001). IQ->associative fluency b=.84; working memory->IQ b=.70. Divergent-convergent latent r=-.52, ns. ATTA creativity index vs RAT r=.09 ns.
limits: One sample, correlational, CFI .82-.91 (modest fit in some models). Convergent measured by RAT/insight tasks only.
agent_relevance: Generation and convergence are separable skills and both rest on association; test them separately in agent evals instead of one 'creativity' score.

source: Beaty, Benedek, Silvia & Schacter (2016) Creative cognition and brain network dynamics. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 20(2)
finding: Neural version of the dual view: the default network supplies candidate ideas, the executive control network couples with it to constrain them. Coupling is task-dependent and changes over the course of a response.
numbers: Poets (Liu et al. 2015 fMRI, as reviewed): default and control clusters were negatively correlated during spontaneous generation but correlation rose during revision. PCC coupled early with insula and later with right DLPFC during divergent thinking.
quote: default and control networks contribute to idea generation and selection, respectively
limits: Small fMRI samples; reverse-inference risk; the review lists open questions.
agent_relevance: Supports a time-ordered pipeline: loose generation first, control-constrained revision later, with the switch handled by a separate controller (salience analogue).

source: Beaty, Benedek, Silvia & Schacter (2016) Creative cognition and brain network dynamics. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 20(2) (musical improvisation)
finding: Control-network links depend on the task goal, so control is not a single 'evaluate' switch. For pianists, right DLPFC coupled with motor regions for key constraints and with default regions for emotional goals.
numbers: Qualitative description of one improvisation study; no effect sizes reported in the review.
limits: Single-study basis.
agent_relevance: The goal given to the control step shapes what it does; evaluation criteria must be explicit in the prompt, not generic 'be critical'.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models
finding: On the Divergent Association Task, GPT-4 beat the human mean, GeminiPro matched humans, and no LLM matched the most creative humans.
numbers: 100,000 humans vs many LLMs; 500 generations per LLM. GPT-4 above humans (significant); GeminiPro not different from humans; GPT-4-turbo was worse than GPT-4.
limits: DAT measures only semantic distance (novelty), not usefulness. High word repetition across runs: 'microscope' in 70% of GPT-4 sets; 'ocean' in over 90% of GPT-4-turbo sets; humans' top word 'car' 1.4%.
agent_relevance: Per-sample scores hide low diversity across samples. The scaffold should measure diversity across calls, not just per output.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models (temperature)
finding: Sampling temperature acts like a generative-mode dial. Higher temperature raised DAT scores and cut word repetition.
numbers: GPT-4, n=500 per condition, temperatures 0.5, 1.0, 1.5; mean DAT at highest setting 85.6, higher than 72% of humans.
limits: Only one model's temperature sweep; usefulness not measured by the DAT.
agent_relevance: Mode switch can be implemented as a temperature change by code: hot for generation, cold for evaluation. See b22 for the quality cost at high temperature.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models (prompt strategy)
finding: Telling the model which strategy to use changed scores: an 'etymology' strategy beat the original DAT prompt for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, and a 'thesaurus' strategy beat it for GPT-4.
numbers: Differences significant except one contrast; exact means only in figures, not extracted.
limits: Strategy effects are task-specific; the opposition strategy behaved as expected.
agent_relevance: Operators that impose a retrieval strategy (a code-chosen lens) are a cheap way to push generation mode.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Benchmarking language model creativity: a case study on code generation. NAACL
finding: Reasoning strategies built for accuracy raise convergent creativity but do not raise divergent creativity, except MCTS. No strategy improved both at once.
numbers: Four strategies tested: MCTS (CodeGemma-7B), self-correction, planning, sampling (GPT-3.5); k=5 samples per problem. Self-correction and planning lowered divergent creativity (diff as low as -1.2 at some states).
quote: None of the four reasoning strategies have been able to simultaneously improve both convergent and divergent creativity
limits: Code-generation on Codeforces tasks only; small models for some arms.
agent_relevance: Single-path refinement (self-critique) narrows output; only multi-path search widens. Evaluation steps may cost divergence, so run them as a separate stage on a pool.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Benchmarking language model creativity: a case study on code generation. NAACL (Denial Prompting)
finding: Denial Prompting (iteratively ban techniques used in the previous solution) forces new strategies. Even GPT-4 stays below human creativity on the combined NeoGauge score.
numbers: Codeforces problems, human solutions as reference. Per-model NeoGauge values in tables not extracted.
limits: Benchmark depends on the pool of human solutions.
agent_relevance: A code-level 'forbid what you just used' operator is a tested way to drive generation away from the obvious mode.

source: Padmakumar et al. (2026, ICLR) Measuring LLM novelty as the frontier of original and high-quality output
finding: Novelty must combine originality (unseen n-grams) and quality. Scale and post-training raise novelty through quality; some base models are less novel than human web text.
numbers: Metric = harmonic mean of unseen-n-gram fraction and task quality. Tested OLMo, OLMo-2, Pythia on story completion, poetry, MacGyver tool use.
limits: Open-data models only; n-gram originality is a proxy.
agent_relevance: Generation-only pressure raises originality but hurts quality. We need an evaluator stage that scores both.

source: Padmakumar et al. (2026, ICLR) Measuring LLM novelty as the frontier of original and high-quality output (temperature)
finding: Temperature has a U-shaped effect on novelty: originality rises monotonically but quality falls, so novelty peaks then declines, and the peak varies by task and model.
numbers: Temperatures 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2.0 on OLMo-7B and Pythia-12B across TinyStories, CoPoet, MacGyver.
limits: Base-model tests; the peak was not constant.
agent_relevance: Cold evaluation after hot generation is needed; tune temperature per task. Contrast b17 where only novelty was measured.

source: Padmakumar et al. (2026, ICLR) Measuring LLM novelty as the frontier of original and high-quality output (prompting interventions)
finding: Asking for novelty and Denial Prompting give modest, uneven gains: they raise originality at the expense of quality.
numbers: Relative novelty change: TinyStories +6.9% (OLMo) and +6.3% (OLMo-2); CoPoet +9.6% and +4.9%; MacGyver -18% (OLMo) and +3.7% (OLMo-2).
limits: Instruction-tuned OLMo variants only; effects far smaller than from scaling.
agent_relevance: Prompting a mode switch is weak. Prefer structural switches (separate calls, filtering) to 'be creative' instructions.

source: Nguyen, Tschiatschek & Singla (2026) CreativeDC: two-stage divergent-convergent prompting for diverse LLM task generation
finding: Splitting a prompt into an exploration stage then a requirement-satisfaction stage raised effective diversity over baseline and chain-of-thought prompting, with higher utility ratings.
numbers: Qwen3-235B-A22B at temperature 1.0. At K=50 tasks: about 12 distinct high-utility tasks vs about 8 for CoT and Base (Vendi score, p<0.001 Bonferroni Wilcoxon). Experts (3) clustered about 16 vs 9 clusters. Expert novelty pairwise win rate 96.67% (SE 2.32); interestingness 0.81 vs 0.50.
limits: Single model, one domain (Python tasks), 3 experts, one concept ('Variables'). CoT and Base were statistically equal, so step-by-step reasoning alone did not help.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a code-enforced two-phase generate-then-constrain flow. Plain CoT adds no diversity.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) with Nieuwenstein et al. (2015), cross-reading
finding: A small robust incubation benefit for open-ended problems coexists with a failed replication of the unconscious-thought advantage in choice. Incubation helps generation breadth; unconscious deliberation does not improve choice.
numbers: Incubation g about 0.29-0.36 (k=117) vs unconscious thought g about 0.15 before bias correction and null in N=399.
limits: Different tasks and paradigms; cross-literature inference.
agent_relevance: Spend the pause budget on generation, not on choosing among options.

source: Benedek et al. 2014 vs Lee & Therriault 2013, comparison
finding: Two latent-variable studies differ on how direct intelligence is. Benedek: EFs explain 43% of Gf-creativity shared variance. Lee: IQ affects divergent thinking only indirectly via associative fluency (indirect b=.46).
numbers: Benedek residual r .45->.34; Lee IQ->divergent indirect b=.46, convergent indirect b=.77, divergent-convergent latent r=-.52 ns.
limits: Different task batteries, samples (about 230 vs 265) and model fit; no preregistered replication found.
agent_relevance: Moderator evidence is thin and model-dependent; do not tune the scaffold around a single latent-variable account.

source: Nusbaum & Silvia (2011) Are intelligence and creativity really so different?
finding: As reported in search summaries: fluid intelligence predicts divergent thinking, partly through executive switching and strategy use; a strategy instruction raised performance.
numbers: Not extracted; only secondary summaries seen.
limits: Not opened this session. Treat as a lead.
agent_relevance: Check original before citing numbers; supports instruction-driven strategy operators.

source: Said-Metwaly et al. (2017) meta-analysis of explicit instructions on divergent thinking
finding: Lead only: instruction effects on divergent thinking are a known moderator in the human literature.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened; no URL verified.
agent_relevance: Worth fetching next pass since it bears on prompt-level mode switching.

source: Gerwig et al. (2021) The relationship between intelligence and divergent thinking: a meta-analytic update. J. Intelligence 9(2)
finding: Lead only: meta-analytic update on intelligence and divergent thinking.
numbers: Not extracted; MDPI blocked access (HTTP 403).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Fetch from another mirror to get moderator effects (scoring, instructions).
